Looking at the premises:

1. ((S ∨ P) ↔ (S ↔ P))
2. (R ↔ Q)

**Analyzing Premise 1:**

Let me evaluate when (S ∨ P) ↔ (S ↔ P) holds:

| S | P | S∨P | S↔P | (S∨P)↔(S↔P) |
|---|---|------|------|-------------|
| T | T |  T  |  T  |     T       |
| T | F |  T  |  F  |     F       |
| F | T |  T  |  F  |     F       |
| F | F |  F  |  T  |     F       |

The biconditional is **only true** when both S and P are true. This means premise 1 is logically equivalent to **S ∧ P**.

**Premise 2** simply states R ↔ Q.

The key conclusion derived from the premises is that both S and P must be true.

<answer>(S ∧ P) ∧ (R ↔ Q)</answer>
